(CNN) -- At 51 years of age, Polish prime minister Donald Tusk has come a long way. As part of the Kashubian minority living in the Gdansk Region, he was born to working-class parents -- his father a carpenter and his mother a nurse. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk was elected in November 2007. As a student of History at the University of Gdansk in the late 1970s, a period of growing discontent with the Communist regime in Poland, he became actively involved in the creation of the opposition Students' Solidarity Committee, founded in reaction to the murder of student activist Stanislaw Pyjas by the State Security Service. Despite his anti-communist activities, he successfully finished his studies in 1980 and joined the Independent Solidarity Trade Union movement. When the Communists imposed martial law in 1981 he continued with his underground activities, writing pamphlets about the ideas of liberal economist Friedrich Hayek and the concept of private property. His heroes became former U.S. president Ronald Reagan and British prime minister Margaret Thatcher. With the fall of Communism in 1989, the Solidarity Movement splintered. Lech Walesa, the former Solidarity Leader was elected President, while Tusk went on to co-found the KLD (Liberal and Democratic Congress Party) with other well-known figures. The Party stood for among other things: free market economy, privatization, individual freedom of Polish citizens and Polish accession to the EU. The following year, during the 1991 Parliamentary elections, the KLD won 37 seats in the lower house of the Polish Parliament. Not being able to follow up on their success in the 1993 elections, the KLD merged with the larger Democratic Union Party (UD) to form a new party called Freedom Union (UW). Tusk soon became Deputy Chairman and in the 1997 elections, he was voted into the Senate. In 2001, Tusk formed the Civic Platform Party (PO), winning seats in that year's parliamentary elections and becoming Deputy Speaker in parliament. But the Civic Platform was not able to sustain its success in the 2005 elections. Tusk and his party lost both the presidential and parliamentary elections to Lech Kacczynski's PiS (Law and Justice Party). This setback was not to last as Tusk triumphed over Jaroslaw Kaczynsky's PiS in the October 2007 elections and became prime minister of Poland. Tusk's economic policies are pro-business: less bureaucratic hurdles and state interference making it easier for entrepreneurs to start businesses. He is also trying to woo back more than a million Poles who left the country to work in other European Union countries after it joined the EU in 2004. Tusk is a keen footballer, viewed in his youth as a promising striker. He is married to historian Malgorzata and has two children, Kasia and Michal.

counterfactuals.output:
## Donald Tusk: Poland’s pro-European political survivor

Donald Tusk, Poland’s prime minister and one of Europe’s most recognizable centrist leaders, has spent much of his political life at the intersection of national transformation and continental politics. A former anti-communist activist, co-founder of Poland’s dominant liberal-conservative party, and ex-president of the European Council, Tusk returned to power in 2023 pledging to restore democratic norms, repair ties with the European Union, and steer Poland back toward the European mainstream.

### Early life and background

Donald Franciszek Tusk was born on April 22, 1957, in Gdańsk, a Baltic port city that would become central to Poland’s anti-communist movement. He comes from a Kashubian family, an ethnic and cultural minority in northern Poland with its own distinct language and traditions. Tusk has often referred to his Kashubian identity as an important part of his background.

His family history was shaped by the turbulence of 20th-century Europe. Like many people from the region, his relatives lived through occupation, war, and shifting borders. Tusk studied history at the University of Gdańsk, where he became politically active during the final decades of communist rule.

### Anti-communist activism

Tusk came of age politically in the shadow of the Solidarity movement, the independent trade union founded in Gdańsk in 1980 and led by Lech Wałęsa. Solidarity became the first mass challenge to communist rule in the Eastern Bloc and helped lay the groundwork for Poland’s eventual transition to democracy.

As a student, Tusk was involved in opposition circles and independent publishing, part of the underground ecosystem that challenged state censorship. During the 1980s, after martial law was imposed by the communist authorities, he remained active in anti-communist networks.

His early activism helped define the political identity he would later carry into elected office: pro-democracy, anti-authoritarian, skeptical of state overreach, and strongly oriented toward the West.

### Rise in Polish politics

After the fall of communism in 1989, Tusk entered mainstream politics. He was among the founders of the Liberal Democratic Congress, a pro-market party that reflected the optimism and upheaval of Poland’s early democratic transition. He later helped form the Freedom Union before becoming one of the principal founders of Civic Platform, known in Polish as Platforma Obywatelska, in 2001.

Civic Platform grew into Poland’s major center-right and liberal-conservative force, promoting economic modernization, European integration, and a more restrained role for the state.

Tusk served in parliament and became a leading opposition figure. In 2005, he ran for president but lost to Lech Kaczyński. Two years later, he led Civic Platform to victory in parliamentary elections, becoming prime minister in 2007.

### First term as prime minister

Tusk served as Poland’s prime minister from 2007 to 2014, making him one of the longest-serving heads of government in the country’s post-communist history. His government emphasized steady economic growth, infrastructure development, and close cooperation with the European Union.

Poland weathered the 2008 global financial crisis better than many European countries, avoiding recession while much of the continent contracted. Tusk’s supporters credited prudent economic management, EU funds, and market-friendly policies. Critics argued that growth did not benefit all regions equally and accused his government of being too technocratic and cautious.

During his premiership, Poland co-hosted the UEFA Euro 2012 football championship with Ukraine, a high-profile event that showcased new roads, stadiums, and infrastructure projects funded in part by EU money.

### European Council president

In 2014, Tusk left Polish politics to become president of the European Council, one of the European Union’s top leadership positions. He held the post until 2019.

His tenure coincided with some of the EU’s most difficult crises, including the eurozone’s continuing strains, the migration crisis, Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, and Brexit. Tusk was often blunt in his defense of European unity and liberal democracy. He also became a prominent critic of Brexit, warning that the United Kingdom’s departure would weaken both Britain and Europe.

His years in Brussels strengthened his reputation as a pro-European statesman and deepened his conflict with Poland’s nationalist Law and Justice party, known as PiS, which governed Poland from 2015 to 2023 and frequently clashed with EU institutions over rule-of-law concerns.

### Return to Polish politics

Tusk returned to domestic politics in 2021 to lead Civic Platform and rebuild Poland’s fragmented opposition. His comeback was polarizing. Supporters saw him as the opposition’s most experienced and internationally respected figure; opponents portrayed him as an out-of-touch Brussels insider.

In the 2023 parliamentary elections, a coalition of opposition parties won enough seats to remove Law and Justice from power. Tusk became prime minister again in December 2023, heading a broad coalition that includes centrists, liberals, conservatives, agrarians, and the left.

His government has focused on restoring judicial independence, unblocking EU funds, improving relations with Brussels, and reversing what it describes as years of democratic backsliding under PiS. Those efforts have faced resistance from political opponents and from institutions reshaped during the previous government’s rule.

### Economic views

Tusk is generally associated with pro-market, pro-European economic policies. He has favored fiscal caution, private enterprise, foreign investment, and integration with EU markets. His approach is often described as pragmatic rather than ideological: supportive of capitalism and competition, but willing to use the state to fund infrastructure and social priorities.

During his earlier time in office, his governments were seen as business-friendly and focused on macroeconomic stability. Critics on the left faulted him for insufficient attention to inequality and public services, while critics on the right accused him of excessive dependence on EU institutions and Western European priorities.

In his more recent political platform, Tusk has combined market-oriented instincts with promises to protect social benefits introduced under Law and Justice, reflecting the changed expectations of Polish voters. His current government has sought to balance fiscal responsibility with commitments on wages, families, healthcare, and defense.

### Foreign policy and security

Tusk is firmly pro-NATO and pro-EU. Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 reinforced Poland’s central role in European security, and Tusk has supported continued aid to Ukraine while also navigating domestic tensions over trade, agriculture, and refugee support.

He has argued that Poland’s security depends on strong alliances, a united Europe, and a close relationship with the United States. At the same time, his return to office marked a shift in tone from the confrontational EU policy of the PiS years toward a more cooperative approach.

### Personal life

Tusk is married to Małgorzata Tusk. The couple have two children. His son, Michał, has worked in journalism and public relations, while his daughter, Katarzyna, is known as a lifestyle blogger and author.

Tusk is also known for his passion for football, a sport he has played recreationally for many years. His public image often blends the traits of a disciplined political operator with those of a combative campaigner. Admirers see him as resilient, strategic, and deeply committed to Poland’s place in Europe. Critics view him as polarizing and too closely tied to the liberal establishment.

### A defining figure in modern Poland

Few Polish politicians have had careers as long or as consequential as Donald Tusk’s. From student opposition activist in communist-era Gdańsk to prime minister, European Council president, and prime minister again, his trajectory mirrors Poland’s own post-1989 journey: from authoritarian rule to democracy, from economic transition to EU membership, and from national debates over sovereignty to broader struggles over the future of Europe.

As he leads Poland for a second time, Tusk faces a difficult task: holding together a diverse coalition, restoring trust in state institutions, managing economic pressures, and maintaining Poland’s influence at a moment of war and uncertainty on Europe’s eastern flank.

## Donald Tusk: From Solidarity Activist to European Statesman

Donald Tusk is one of the most influential Polish politicians of the post-communist era. His career has spanned underground opposition activity, liberal party-building, national leadership, and high office in the European Union. Known for his pro-European outlook, pragmatic liberalism, and support for market-oriented reforms, Tusk rose from the anti-communist milieu of Gdańsk to become Poland’s prime minister and later president of the European Council.

### Early Life and the Solidarity Movement

Donald Franciszek Tusk was born on April 22, 1957, in Gdańsk, a port city that played a central role in Poland’s modern political history. Gdańsk was the birthplace of the Solidarity movement, the independent trade union that emerged in 1980 under the leadership of Lech Wałęsa and became the most important opposition force against communist rule in Poland.

Tusk studied history at the University of Gdańsk, where he became involved in opposition circles. During the late 1970s and 1980s, he participated in anti-communist activities and supported Solidarity. Like many activists of his generation, Tusk’s political identity was shaped by resistance to authoritarian rule, the struggle for civil liberties, and the desire to integrate Poland with democratic Europe.

After martial law was imposed in Poland in December 1981, Solidarity was suppressed, but opposition networks continued underground. Tusk remained connected to independent publishing and political activism, helping to sustain the civic and intellectual foundations of Poland’s democratic transition.

### The Liberal Turn: Founding the KLD

Following the collapse of communist rule in 1989, Tusk became part of a generation of activists who sought to define Poland’s new political and economic order. He emerged as a leading figure in the liberal current of Polish politics, emphasizing private enterprise, decentralization, integration with the West, and a limited role for the state in the economy.

In 1990, Tusk helped found the Liberal Democratic Congress, known by its Polish initials KLD — Kongres Liberalno-Demokratyczny. The party represented a pro-market, pro-Western strand of post-Solidarity politics. It advocated economic liberalization, entrepreneurship, privatization, and closer ties with Western Europe.

The KLD attracted support especially among urban professionals, business-oriented voters, and parts of the new middle class. However, Poland’s early transition years were economically difficult, and liberal reformers often faced public frustration over unemployment, inequality, and the social costs of rapid market transformation.

Tusk served as one of the party’s key leaders and developed a reputation as a disciplined organizer and articulate advocate of liberal democracy. Although the KLD never became a mass party, it was an important stepping stone in Tusk’s political rise and helped establish the ideological foundations of his later career.

### From KLD to Civic Platform

In the mid-1990s, the KLD merged with the Democratic Union to form the Freedom Union, but Tusk eventually moved toward creating a broader center-right formation. In 2001, he co-founded Civic Platform, or Platforma Obywatelska, together with Andrzej Olechowski and Maciej Płażyński.

Civic Platform was designed as a modern, moderate, pro-European party. It combined liberal economic ideas with a centrist political style and sought to appeal to voters who favored stability, Western integration, and competent governance. The party positioned itself as an alternative both to the post-communist left and to more nationalist or socially conservative forces on the right.

Tusk became increasingly central to Civic Platform’s identity. Under his leadership, the party cultivated an image of professionalism and moderation. It supported Poland’s membership in the European Union and NATO, promoted market economics, and appealed strongly to urban voters, professionals, entrepreneurs, and younger Poles who saw their future in a Europeanized Poland.

### The 2005 Setback

The year 2005 was a major test for Tusk. He ran for president of Poland as Civic Platform’s candidate and was widely seen as a serious contender. At the same time, Civic Platform competed in parliamentary elections against Law and Justice, or PiS, a conservative party led by Jarosław Kaczyński and associated with his twin brother, Lech Kaczyński.

Tusk’s campaign emphasized modernization, economic reform, and European-style liberal conservatism. However, he faced criticism from opponents who portrayed him as too elitist, too market-oriented, and insufficiently attentive to social inequality. Law and Justice successfully appealed to voters concerned about corruption, insecurity, and the uneven benefits of the post-1989 transformation.

In the presidential election, Tusk lost to Lech Kaczyński. Civic Platform also finished behind Law and Justice in the parliamentary election. The result was a significant setback: instead of entering government as the dominant force of the center-right, Civic Platform found itself in opposition.

Yet the defeat proved formative. Tusk learned from the campaign and adjusted his political approach. He placed greater emphasis on social reassurance, political discipline, and presenting Civic Platform as a party capable not only of reform but also of responsible governance.

### The 2007 Victory

Tusk’s opportunity came sooner than expected. The Law and Justice-led government formed after 2005 became increasingly polarizing, and early parliamentary elections were called in 2007. Civic Platform ran a strong campaign focused on stability, modernization, and ending political conflict.

In the 2007 election, Tusk led Civic Platform to victory. The party won the largest share of the vote and formed a coalition government with the Polish People’s Party, a centrist agrarian party. Tusk became prime minister in November 2007.

His victory marked a turning point in Polish politics. Civic Platform’s success reflected the strength of Poland’s urban middle class, the appeal of EU-oriented modernization, and fatigue with the confrontational style of the previous government. Tusk presented himself as a pragmatic leader focused on economic growth, European cooperation, and administrative competence rather than ideological battles.

### Pro-Business and Market-Oriented Policies

As prime minister, Tusk pursued broadly pro-business and market-friendly policies. His government emphasized fiscal discipline, infrastructure development, support for entrepreneurship, and Poland’s integration into the European economy. While not as radically liberal as some of the KLD’s early post-communist ideas, Tusk’s administration favored a predictable business climate and sought to attract investment.

One of the defining features of his premiership was economic stability. During the global financial crisis of 2008–2009, Poland was the only European Union member state to avoid recession, a fact often highlighted by Tusk and his supporters. This outcome reflected several factors, including domestic demand, a flexible currency, EU funds, banking-sector caution, and government policy.

Tusk’s governments invested heavily in infrastructure, especially roads, highways, railways, and preparations for Poland’s co-hosting of the UEFA Euro 2012 football championship with Ukraine. EU structural funds played a major role in financing modernization projects, and Tusk’s pro-European stance helped align Poland closely with Brussels.

His administration also supported gradual privatization and efforts to reduce bureaucratic barriers for businesses. However, his reforms were often pragmatic rather than revolutionary. Critics argued that Civic Platform promised more economic liberalization than it delivered, while supporters contended that Tusk balanced reform with social and political realities.

Tusk also raised the retirement age, a controversial move intended to address long-term demographic and fiscal pressures. The policy was praised by some economists as responsible but criticized by opponents as socially insensitive. It later became one of the issues used by Law and Justice to mobilize voters against Civic Platform.

### European Leadership

Tusk’s pro-European reputation eventually carried him beyond Polish politics. In 2014, he was chosen as president of the European Council, one of the European Union’s top positions. He served from 2014 to 2019, representing EU leaders during a turbulent period that included the migration crisis, Brexit negotiations, tensions with Russia after the annexation of Crimea, and internal disputes over the rule of law.

His selection reflected Poland’s growing importance within the EU and Tusk’s image as a mainstream European conservative-liberal politician. As European Council president, he was known for his firm stance toward Russia, his defense of EU unity, and his often sharp criticism of Brexit.

### Legacy and Political Significance

Donald Tusk’s political rise mirrors the broader story of post-communist Poland: the passage from opposition activism to democratic party politics, from economic transition to EU membership, and from national reconstruction to European influence.

His career began in the world of Solidarity and anti-communist resistance. Through the KLD, he helped articulate a liberal, pro-market vision for the new Poland. With Civic Platform, he built that vision into a major governing force. His 2005 defeat forced him to adapt, while his 2007 victory made him prime minister and one of the central figures in Polish public life.

Tusk remains a polarizing figure. Admirers see him as a modernizer, a skilled political strategist, and a defender of Poland’s European orientation. Critics view him as too close to business interests, insufficiently attentive to social concerns, or overly accommodating to EU institutions. Regardless of perspective, his role in shaping Poland’s post-1989 political landscape is undeniable.

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a detailed profile of Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk, written like a CNN backgrounder, with information on his education, opposition activity under communism, party affiliations, family, and football interests.
counterfactuals.output:
## Donald Tusk: Poland’s pro-European comeback prime minister

Donald Tusk is one of Poland’s most prominent political figures of the post-communist era — a former prime minister, former president of the European Council and longtime leader of the centrist, pro-European opposition to Poland’s national-conservative right. He returned to power as prime minister in December 2023 after an election that ended eight years of rule by the Law and Justice party, known as PiS.

Tusk’s political identity has been shaped by Poland’s transition from communism to democracy, his roots in the Baltic port city of Gdańsk, and his long-running rivalry with Jarosław Kaczyński and the Polish right.

### Early life and education

Donald Franciszek Tusk was born on April 22, 1957, in Gdańsk, a city with a complex Polish-German history and a strong tradition of labor activism. His family background included Kashubian roots — a West Slavic ethnic and linguistic minority concentrated in northern Poland.

Tusk studied history at the University of Gdańsk, graduating in 1980. His studies coincided with a period of mounting opposition to communist rule in Poland, especially along the Baltic coast. Gdańsk was central to that movement: it was the home of the Lenin Shipyard and the birthplace of the Solidarity trade union, which became the most important anti-communist opposition force in the Soviet bloc.

### Opposition activity under communism

As a student and young activist, Tusk was involved in anti-communist circles during the late 1970s and 1980s. He helped organize student opposition activity and was associated with the Independent Students’ Association, a pro-Solidarity student movement.

After the communist authorities imposed martial law in December 1981 in an effort to crush Solidarity, Tusk continued to work in opposition-linked circles. He was involved in underground publishing and journalism, part of the wider network that circulated uncensored political writing and information outside state control.

Tusk later worked as a manual laborer, including in industrial rope-access and chimney-painting jobs — the kind of employment taken by some opposition activists who found more conventional professional paths blocked or politically constrained under the communist system.

His anti-communist credentials became an important part of his later political biography, though he would come to represent a more liberal, technocratic and European-oriented wing of the post-Solidarity political spectrum.

### Political rise and party affiliations

Tusk entered national politics after the fall of communism and became associated with Poland’s liberal and conservative-liberal movements.

In the early 1990s, he co-founded the Liberal Democratic Congress, or KLD, a free-market, pro-Western party that favored economic liberalization and integration with European institutions. The KLD later merged into the Freedom Union, a centrist liberal party that played a significant role in Poland’s early democratic politics.

In 2001, Tusk co-founded Civic Platform, known in Polish as Platforma Obywatelska, or PO. The party became the main center-right and later centrist liberal alternative to PiS. Civic Platform advocated closer ties with the European Union, market-friendly economic policies, and a more moderate social and institutional agenda than the nationalist-conservative right.

Tusk served as prime minister of Poland from 2007 to 2014, leading Civic Platform to two consecutive parliamentary election victories — a notable achievement in Polish politics. His first stint in office was marked by steady economic growth, a pro-EU foreign policy and major preparations for Poland’s co-hosting of the Euro 2012 football championship with Ukraine.

In 2014, Tusk left Polish politics to become president of the European Council, one of the European Union’s top leadership posts. He held the role from 2014 to 2019, representing the EU’s heads of state and government during a turbulent period that included the migration crisis, Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, and the Brexit negotiations.

After leaving the European Council, Tusk became president of the European People’s Party, the main center-right political family in the EU. He later returned to Polish domestic politics, retaking the leadership of Civic Platform and becoming the most visible figure in the opposition to PiS.

Following Poland’s 2023 parliamentary election, Tusk formed a coalition government made up of Civic Coalition, the centrist Third Way alliance and The Left. He was sworn in again as prime minister in December 2023.

### Rivalry with Law and Justice

Much of Tusk’s modern political career has been defined by his rivalry with Law and Justice and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. The divide is both ideological and personal, reflecting broader tensions in Polish society over the rule of law, media freedom, national identity, Catholic social values, economic redistribution and Poland’s relationship with Brussels.

PiS has long portrayed Tusk as too close to Germany and EU elites, while Tusk has accused PiS of undermining democratic institutions, politicizing the judiciary and isolating Poland within Europe. His return to office was widely seen as an attempt to restore Poland’s influence in the EU and reverse some of PiS’s institutional changes.

### Family

Tusk is married to Małgorzata Tusk. The couple have two children: a son, Michał, and a daughter, Katarzyna.

His family has occasionally appeared in public discussion, as is common for major political figures in Poland. Katarzyna Tusk became known in her own right as a lifestyle blogger and author. Michał Tusk has worked as a journalist and in the transport sector and has at times been drawn into political controversies involving his father’s opponents.

Tusk has often spoken about his Gdańsk upbringing and family history, including the experience of living in a region shaped by shifting borders, wartime trauma and postwar communist rule.

### Football interests

Tusk is well known as an avid football fan and amateur player. Football has been a recurring part of his public image: he has often presented himself as someone who enjoys playing the game rather than merely watching it from the stands.

He supports Lechia Gdańsk, the main football club of his hometown. His association with the sport has sometimes served as a softer counterpoint to his image as a hard-edged political operator. During his first premiership, Poland’s co-hosting of Euro 2012 was one of the major national projects linked to his government, involving stadium construction, infrastructure upgrades and international visibility for Poland.

Tusk has also been known to participate in informal football matches with colleagues and political associates, reinforcing his reputation as a politician with a genuine personal attachment to the sport.

### Political image

Tusk’s supporters see him as a pragmatic pro-European leader who helped anchor Poland in the Western mainstream and restore its voice in EU politics. His critics cast him as elitist, overly accommodating to Brussels and Berlin, and insufficiently attentive to conservative and rural voters.

After decades in public life, he remains one of the most polarizing and consequential politicians in Poland — a figure whose career traces the country’s path from communist rule, through democratic transition, to its present-day battles over Europe, sovereignty and liberal democracy.

counterfactuals.output:
Donald Tusk is a Polish politician who became one of the central figures of post-communist liberal politics in Poland and, in 2007, prime minister.

Born on April 22, 1957, in Gdańsk, Tusk grew up in a Kashubian family, a regional ethnic-cultural minority in northern Poland. His family background and identity remained part of his public image; he has often emphasized his attachment to Gdańsk, Kashubia, and Poland’s democratic traditions. He studied history at the University of Gdańsk, where he became involved in opposition activity during the communist period.

In the 1980s, Tusk was associated with the anti-communist opposition around the Solidarity movement. After the fall of communism in 1989, he entered democratic politics and became a leading advocate of liberal, pro-market, and pro-European ideas. In 1991 he co-founded the Liberal Democratic Congress, a party that supported economic liberalization, privatization, and Poland’s integration with Western institutions. He was elected to parliament in the early 1990s and became known as part of the emerging generation of liberal politicians after communism.

During the 1990s, Tusk’s political camp went through mergers and realignments. The Liberal Democratic Congress joined with other centrist forces to form the Freedom Union, but Tusk eventually broke with it. In 2001 he co-founded Civic Platform, a center-right liberal party, together with Andrzej Olechowski and Maciej Płażyński. Civic Platform promoted a combination of market-oriented economic policy, administrative reform, lower taxes, support for entrepreneurship, and a strongly pro-European foreign policy.

Tusk’s political profile was shaped by his support for Poland’s integration into the European Union and a broadly Atlanticist orientation, favoring close ties with the EU and NATO while presenting Poland as a stable, modern European democracy. Domestically, he advocated a liberal economic agenda: reducing bureaucracy, encouraging private enterprise, improving public finances, and modernizing the state. Civic Platform also appealed to urban, middle-class voters and those who wanted a less confrontational, more pragmatic style of politics than that offered by nationalist or socially conservative rivals.

In 2005, Tusk ran for president of Poland but lost to Lech Kaczyński of the conservative Law and Justice party. The same year, Civic Platform also lost the parliamentary election to Law and Justice, beginning a sharp rivalry between the two parties and between Tusk and the Kaczyński brothers. Tusk remained leader of Civic Platform and positioned it as the main opposition force.

In the 2007 parliamentary election, Civic Platform won the largest share of the vote, campaigning on economic modernization, better governance, European engagement, and a more moderate political style. Tusk then formed a coalition government with the Polish People’s Party and became prime minister of Poland in November 2007. His rise marked the consolidation of liberal, pro-EU politics as a major force in post-communist Poland.
